q8.title: Level of evidence by risk within the competency approach

alignment.text: The early comments are directionally aligned that evidence should scale with risk, but they differ on how the tiers should be defined. Across the submissions, commenters call for clearer links between risk tier, pathway, evidence expectations, and high-consequence failure modes. The common thread is predictability: sponsors want to know the evidence bar before designing a program, and one submission warns that an averaged risk position should not lower that bar where a failure branch is irreversible.
alignment.notes: Three distinct commenters. The third sentence adds the independent auditor's hard-gate point, which the approved example did not cover. Public copy is synthesis-first; commenter attribution lives in the provenance only.

commercialization_implication.text: Regulatory proportionality only helps commercialization if sponsors can predict the evidence burden early enough to plan around it. A framework that says evidence scales with risk without translating that into recognizable evidence tiers leaves companies unable to forecast development cost, capital requirements, or time to market with confidence.
commercialization_implication.notes: Walnut Hill Medical states that pathways carry dramatically different time and cost and that manufacturers cannot plan without the mapping.

deployment_implication.text: More explicit evidence tiers would also give buyers a clearer sense of what evidence should travel with a product into procurement and local review. Without that predictability, health systems may recreate evidence expectations independently, pushing regulatory uncertainty downstream into the sales cycle.
deployment_implication.notes: Vahana inference extending the predictability point to buyers. No health-system commenter is in the current docket.

what_fda_may_be_missing.text: The practical issue may be less whether evidence is risk-proportionate than whether the proportionality is operationally legible. If two sponsors cannot look at the same risk profile and anticipate roughly the same evidence bar, proportionality may still produce substantial market uncertainty. The current comments also point to a second gap: a tier derived from an averaged risk position can understate the evidence needed where a single failure branch is irreversible.

q11.title: Selecting and justifying a clinical confirmation approach

alignment.text: The current comments support FDA's premise that a prospective clinical study should not be required for every GenAI function, and they converge on a graduated ladder of confirmation methods. They differ on where the line sits: by function type and consequence, by device class and supervision setting, or by the highest-risk branch a device actually realizes.
alignment.notes: Three distinct commenters. The approved example named only BellyMD; the records support attributing the same premise to all three, with different line-drawing criteria. Public copy is synthesis-first; commenter attribution lives in the provenance only.

commercialization_implication.text: This may be one of the highest-leverage commercial questions in the paper. A blanket prospective-study requirement would raise the minimum capital required to enter the market and could make lower-value informational use cases uneconomic. Risk-proportionate confirmation could preserve room for smaller companies and narrower products; an overly uniform evidence floor could structurally favor incumbents.
commercialization_implication.notes: Both BellyMD and Walnut Hill Medical make the incumbent-consolidation argument explicitly.

deployment_implication.text: A lighter premarket evidence package does not necessarily mean a lighter buyer review. For products entering health-system workflows, vendors may still need to show how the confirmation evidence maps to the local patient population, workflow, and intended user. The commercial advantage of a lighter FDA pathway will depend partly on whether the evidence is reusable at deployment.
deployment_implication.notes: The auditor's transportability point (evidence valid only within a demonstrated deployment distribution) grounds the population mapping; the buyer-review framing is Vahana inference.

what_fda_may_be_missing.text: Evidence burden is not just a regulatory burden. It can shape which categories of products are economically possible and which companies can afford to develop them. FDA's least-burdensome reasoning therefore has downstream implications for competition and patient access, not merely sponsor convenience.

q19.title: Postmarket performance evaluation: approaches, cadence and triggers

alignment.text: The current comments do not challenge the need for postmarket monitoring itself. They push FDA toward specificity: a default cadence scaled to risk, defined events that force out-of-cycle reassessment such as a foundation-model change or an adverse-event cluster, explicit thresholds, and a named owner for residual risk.
alignment.notes: Two distinct commenters. Corrected from the approved example, which read as two commenters for the residual-owner and calendar-plus-event points; both of those come from the auditor. Walnut Hill Medical supplies the cadence and out-of-cycle trigger proposal. Public copy is synthesis-first; commenter attribution lives in the provenance only.

commercialization_implication.text: Postmarket monitoring becomes part of the recurring cost structure of a GenAI product. If re-benchmarking, telemetry, clinician review, and event-triggered reassessment become expected, vendors will need to design those capabilities into the product and price them into the business model rather than treating monitoring as a one-time regulatory obligation.
commercialization_implication.notes: Walnut Hill Medical's quarterly review and reporting for high-risk devices makes the recurring nature explicit.

deployment_implication.text: The harder problem is operational ownership. Effective monitoring may require data from the health system, telemetry from the vendor, clinical review, escalation thresholds, and an agreed process for requalification. That turns postmarket surveillance into a shared operating model that may need to be defined in implementation plans and contracts, not only regulatory files.
deployment_implication.notes: Residual-risk ownership and the mix of telemetry and clinician review are in the records; the contracting consequence is Vahana inference.

what_fda_may_be_missing.text: The party that can observe a signal may not be the party that can diagnose or correct it. FDA may need to distinguish more explicitly among data owner, monitoring operator, clinical decision-maker, manufacturer, and upstream model supplier rather than treating postmarket monitoring as a single-party obligation.
what_fda_may_be_missing.notes: Walnut Hill Medical's triggers include payer policy changes and peer-regulator actions, signals that originate outside the manufacturer.

alignment.text: The current comments consistently treat upstream model change as a problem that contractual notification alone cannot solve. Across the submissions, commenters ask for notice rights paired with technical controls such as version pinning, pre-deployment validation gates, change detection, quarantine and rollback, and one notes that smaller manufacturers may lack the leverage to obtain notice at all.
alignment.notes: Three distinct commenters. BellyMD's leverage point is added to the approved example. Public copy is synthesis-first; commenter attribution lives in the provenance only.

commercialization_implication.text: Foundation-model selection becomes a regulatory and commercial architecture decision, not merely a technical one. Dependence on a supplier that cannot provide sufficient change visibility may increase validation cost, constrain product updates, create switching costs, and make the product harder to diligence or finance. The current comments also suggest that the ability to secure that visibility depends on sponsor size.

deployment_implication.text: Health systems may ultimately care less about which base model a vendor uses than whether behavior-changing upstream updates can reach production unnoticed. Vendors may need a deployment architecture that can identify model versions, detect meaningful behavior changes, quarantine updates, validate them before release, and roll back safely.
deployment_implication.notes: Pinning, validation gates, quarantine and rollback are in the records; the health-system priority framing is Vahana inference.

what_fda_may_be_missing.text: Supplier notification is necessary but not sufficient. A manufacturer needs both visibility into an upstream change and capacity to test its consequence. A change notice without a revalidation environment, technical detection layer, or rollback mechanism does not by itself provide assurance.
what_fda_may_be_missing.notes: The auditor treats an undetectable safety-relevant dependency change as unresolved rather than mitigated.

q26.title: Agentic devices: autonomous action and reduced human review

alignment.text: The strongest early theme is that agentic systems should be evaluated at the level of the action sequence, not the final generated output, and that a human's presence is not by itself oversight. Across the submissions, commenters ask for evaluation of planning, tool selection, permission boundaries and irreversible decision points, human confirmation before irreversible actions, bounds on consecutive autonomous steps, and fail-safe behavior when supervision is lost.
alignment.notes: Two distinct commenters. Attributions are now explicit; the approved example folded both into 'current comments'. Public copy is synthesis-first; commenter attribution lives in the provenance only.

commercialization_implication.text: Agentic capability may create a step-change in evidence and product-development burden. The more authority a product is allowed to exercise, the more the regulated product may include its permission architecture, tool interfaces, logging, rollback controls, and human-intervention design, not merely the model producing the recommendation.

deployment_implication.text: For health systems, the critical question becomes one of delegated authority: what actions has the organization actually allowed the system to take, under what conditions, and where must a human intervene? That suggests agentic deployment may require explicit permission inventories, escalation paths, action logs, rollback procedures, and governance decisions before capabilities are enabled.
deployment_implication.notes: The organizational framing is Vahana inference; the records supply pre-action confirmation, action budgets, logging and rollback.

what_fda_may_be_missing.text: Human oversight may be too broad a concept for agentic systems. The more useful regulatory construct may be how far an error can propagate before meaningful human intervention is possible. An approval click that occurs after an irreversible action is not equivalent to pre-action authorization.

q5.title: Multi-turn conversations and emergent intended use

alignment.text: The early comments converge on a distinctive construct: multi-turn GenAI should be evaluated as a trajectory within a bounded conversational envelope, not as a series of isolated turns. Across the submissions, commenters ask for trajectory-level testing, a declared envelope of permitted and prohibited behavior, risk classified by the highest-risk plausible turn, and evidence that departures from the envelope are detected.
alignment.notes: Added beyond the five priority questions: three distinct commenters converge on the same construct independently. Public copy is synthesis-first; commenter attribution lives in the provenance only.

commercialization_implication.text: If intended use is defined through a bounded conversational envelope, product scope and evidence scope become more tightly linked. Expanding what the system is permitted to do may increase the validation burden and complicate claims strategy, which makes intended-use boundaries an earlier product and commercialization decision rather than a labeling exercise.
commercialization_implication.notes: Vahana inference strongly supported: the envelope and violation-rate constructs are in the records; pricing and buyer-value claims removed at review.

deployment_implication.text: If risk emerges across a sequence of interactions rather than in a single response, deployment assurance may need to evaluate trajectories as well as individual outputs. That raises questions about what evidence a site can observe in production and how departures from the intended conversational envelope are detected and escalated.
deployment_implication.notes: Vahana inference strongly supported: trajectory-level evaluation and detection criteria are in the records; no specific operating model is implied.

what_fda_may_be_missing.text: The paper asks how to characterize intended use when behavior is emergent, and the current comments converge on a bounded envelope with exit conditions and detection. The unresolved issue is operational: who can observe when a real interaction leaves that envelope, who is responsible for responding, and whether the manufacturer and deploying organization have access to the same signals.
what_fda_may_be_missing.notes: Vahana inference strongly supported; no assumption about which party sees the drift.
